title: US Employers Brace for Labor Crisis as 350,000 Haitians Face Loss of Work Permits Under TPS Ruling
excerpt: Healthcare providers, elder care agencies and manufacturers warn of cascading workforce gaps as the Supreme Court upholds termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haitian nationals.
body:
• Roughly 350,000 Haitian TPS holders could lose their work authorization after the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end their protections.
  • Healthcare and elder care providers, particularly in Florida and New York, say the loss of trained caregivers will worsen an already severe staffing shortage.
  • Haitian TPS holders contribute an estimated $6 billion annually to the US economy, with 200,000 working in industries already facing labor gaps.
  • A federal judge has temporarily delayed the work permit expiration to July 27, but the long-term outlook remains uncertain.

A Workforce Cliff for Healthcare

The numbers sound abstract until they land at a nursing home's front desk. Across Florida, New York and other states with large Haitian communities, healthcare providers are watching the calendar with growing alarm as work permits for Temporary Protected Status holders edge toward expiration.

About 350,000 Haitian nationals currently hold TPS in the United States, with roughly half based in Florida. The Supreme Court's ruling last month upheld the Trump administration's authority to terminate TPS designations it deems no longer necessary, calling the move a "tremendous win" for immigration enforcement.

But employers see something different: a workforce cliff. In Rockland County, New York, the disability services agency Jawonio reports that 22% of its workforce are Haitian TPS recipients — direct support professionals who provide round-the-clock care for adults with developmental disabilities. At St. Dominic's Family Services, the vacancy rate for similar positions already stands at 28%, even before any TPS-related departures.

"It's like firing your best worker for no apparent reason."

— Sabine French, whose 91-year-old mother depends on a Haitian home care aide

$6 Billion in Economic Output at Risk

According to FWD.us, an immigration policy organization, Haitian TPS holders contribute nearly $6 billion annually to the US economy. Some 200,000 of them work in industries already facing chronic labor shortages — healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing and construction.

The Florida Restaurant & Lodging Association, alongside the National Restaurant Association and 11 state counterparts, has urged the Department of Homeland Security to provide a 90- to 120-day transition period, clear guidance on employment verification, and protections for employers acting in good faith. In South Florida alone, the 93,000 Haitian TPS holders contribute an estimated $2.6 billion annually to the state economy.

Elder care has emerged as the sector most immediately vulnerable. Carole Hirsch, who runs an emergency companion care agency in West Palm Beach, predicts that nursing homes and home care agencies will be forced to hire less qualified workers at higher costs. "Good aides are $30 to $45 an hour now, compared to $18 to $20 when I started 20 years ago," she told the Palm Beach Post. "They are caught in a trap."

Legal Limbo Continues

A federal judge in Boston temporarily extended work authorization to July 27 after plaintiffs argued that USCIS had unlawfully implemented new restrictions, including retroactively applying a 2025 law's provisions to TPS holders from El Salvador, Sudan and Ukraine. The ruling, issued by Judge Gorton — an appointee of President George H.W. Bush — prevents the stripping of work permits while courts consider the broader legality of the administration's approach.

The Trump administration maintains that TPS was "always meant to be temporary" and accuses prior administrations of allowing it to function as "de facto amnesty." DHS has urged individuals who no longer qualify to pursue other lawful status, depart voluntarily or face removal proceedings.

Implications for the Indian Diaspora

While the immediate crisis centres on Haitian nationals, the TPS upheaval carries broader signals for Indian immigrants navigating the US system. TPS has historically covered nationals from countries facing armed conflict, natural disasters or other extraordinary conditions — a framework that could theoretically apply to future Indian designees.

More directly, the administration's aggressive posture on immigration enforcement — from the $100,000 H-1B fee proposal to tighter student visa rules — reflects a political environment in which all categories of immigration status face heightened scrutiny. Indian green card holders and H-1B workers watching the TPS situation are reading a warning about the fragility of status-dependent work authorization in the current policy landscape.

What's Next

Lawyers for the Haitian plaintiffs have indicated they could file an amended lawsuit by July 31. An estimated 25,000 US citizen children of Haitian TPS holders face the prospect of being pushed into poverty if their parents lose work authorization. For employers, the question is not philosophical but logistical: who fills the shifts that keep hospitals, nursing homes and farms running?
nri_angle: The TPS upheaval signals a broader tightening of status-dependent work authorization that Indian H-1B holders and green card applicants are watching closely.
